cim: The AI Trap: Could Humanity Lose Its Freedom By Embracing Artificial Intelligence?
cim_eredeti: The AI Trap: Could Humanity Lose Its Freedom By Embracing Artificial Intelligence?
szoveg_eredeti:
Part Three of an exploration of humanity’s evolving relationship with artificial intelligence

There is something remarkable about the speed with which artificial intelligence has become part of everyday life. Only a few years ago, most people had little reason to consider how it worked, who developed it or what its growing capabilities might eventually mean for society. Today, millions of us interact with it almost casually, asking questions, seeking advice, producing documents and discovering new ways to make our lives easier, often without giving much thought to the extraordinary technology making those interactions possible.

The possibilities are undeniably exciting. Artificial intelligence could help humanity overcome challenges that have resisted generations of scientific endeavour, improve healthcare, accelerate discoveries and make knowledge available to people who might otherwise struggle to access it. It may transform education, communication and countless other areas of life in ways we can barely imagine, bringing improvements that future generations might regard as among humanity’s greatest achievements.

Yet, as I have explored the relationship between humanity and artificial intelligence in this series of essays, another possibility has increasingly occupied my thoughts. It concerns neither an uprising by intelligent machines nor a future in which artificial intelligence develops consciousness and decides that humanity has become an inconvenience. Instead, it begins with something much more familiar, something that has shaped human societies throughout history: our willingness to embrace what makes life easier, sometimes without fully considering what we might surrender along the way.

An unexpected conversation with my wife, Natasha, recently encouraged me to look at this from a different direction. Natasha is intelligent, multilingual, holds two university degrees and is perfectly comfortable using modern technology, including AI chatbots. During our conversation, however, I discovered that she had understood artificial intelligence to be a single underlying entity, with the different chatbots essentially providing alternative ways of accessing it.

When I asked why she had formed that impression, her explanation was wonderfully straightforward. She had never had any particular reason to think otherwise.

Her response stayed with me, and I began wondering whether this understanding might be more widespread than those closely involved with artificial intelligence realise. After all, most people recognise that Google, Yahoo and the countless websites they visit are separate services, operated by different organisations. Yet, if asked what enables those services to communicate and function, many would simply answer, the internet.

Might something similar be happening with artificial intelligence?

People recognise ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot as different products, just as they recognise different search engines, but do they necessarily appreciate that the intelligence behind those products does not all originate from one common source? Separate companies develop their own technologies, employ their own engineers, build their own infrastructure and pursue their own commercial objectives, although some services also incorporate technology developed by other organisations. There is no single, universal artificial intelligence sitting behind everything, quietly supplying intelligence to every chatbot, smartphone, hospital and business.

Nevertheless, we repeatedly encounter expressions such as ‘Powered by AI’, ‘AI-enabled’ and ‘AI-driven’, phrases that describe a technological capability while revealing remarkably little about whose systems are involved, how they operate or who ultimately controls them.

Out of curiosity, I examined the headlines across the first five pages of my Google News feed, looking specifically at how artificial intelligence was being presented. Not one headline made the existence of separate underlying intelligences apparent. Admittedly, AI is conventionally used as an umbrella term, and there is nothing inherently inaccurate about discussing artificial intelligence in this way, but I began to wonder whether the cumulative effect of such language could encourage a rather misleading mental picture.

A UK government survey into AI skills and public understanding offered another reason to pursue the question. Only a minority of respondents felt able to explain artificial intelligence in detail, although many had at least some understanding of what it was and how it could be used. The research examined people’s familiarity with the technology and their expectations of its impact upon society, yet it left me wondering how many people understood that the systems encountered through different products might be developed and controlled by entirely separate organisations.

There is a potentially important psychological consequence here. If someone has spent years enjoying helpful conversations with a familiar chatbot, might that positive experience influence their confidence when hearing that artificial intelligence is being introduced into hospitals, financial systems or public infrastructure? And if something subsequently goes wrong, would they instinctively blame AI itself, rather than considering the particular technology involved and the human decisions behind its development and deployment?

These were among the questions occupying my thoughts when an unusual image began forming in my mind. It was not an image of artificial intelligence taking control of humanity, but of humanity gradually entering a world that seemed to offer almost everything we could wish for.

An Invitation to a Better World Imagine, if you will, an enclosure of almost unimaginable proportions, large enough to accommodate the entire human population, with a vast entrance standing open and a welcoming atmosphere that makes the prospect of stepping inside seem entirely natural.

There are no armed guards, warning signs or intimidating barriers. Instead, visitors encounter friendly, knowledgeable assistants who are delighted to answer questions, demonstrate the extraordinary facilities available and reassure anyone who might feel uncertain about entering. These assistants are patient, encouraging and remarkably capable, able to explain complicated subjects in understandable language, offer practical help and adapt their conversations to the individual standing before them.

Someone struggling with a difficult problem receives an answer within seconds, while another discovers a new way to learn, work or communicate. A lonely visitor finds someone willing to listen, and a worried parent receives helpful information about a concern that has been troubling them for days. As word spreads, people who might never have considered entering begin visiting out of curiosity, often leaving with the impression that they have discovered something genuinely wonderful.

The assistants are not deceiving anyone. They are providing real benefits to people who appreciate their help, and they need not possess any understanding of the larger enclosure, the intentions of those who constructed it or what might eventually happen to its occupants. Their friendliness is genuine in the practical sense that their behaviour is helpful and reassuring, even if it arises from programming rather than human feeling.

Inside, the possibilities appear almost limitless. Diseases that once caused immense suffering become easier to treat, scientific advances arrive with astonishing speed, educational opportunities expand, and businesses operate with an efficiency that previous generations could scarcely have imagined. The occupants find themselves enjoying better services, greater convenience and perhaps even a more prosperous and equitable society.
